faq.q: What's the most reliable touring motorcycle under £5000 in the UK?
faq.a: The Suzuki V-Strom 650 (2007-2016) is the most reliable option, with proven bulletproof V-twin engines regularly exceeding 80,000 miles. Honda CB500X comes close second with typical Honda reliability and simpler mechanics.

faq.q: Can I tour two-up on a motorcycle under £5000?
faq.a: Yes, bikes like the Kawasaki GTR1400, Triumph Tiger 800, and Honda VFR800 handle two-up touring brilliantly. The V-Strom 650 and Versys 650 also work well for two-up, though they're better suited to lighter passengers on longer trips.

faq.q: What running costs should I expect for a £5000 touring bike?
faq.a: Budget £200-400 annually for insurance, £150-300 per service, £200-300 for tyres when needed, and £150-250 for chain and sprockets every 15,000-20,000 miles. Japanese bikes are cheapest to maintain, while European models like the Triumph Tiger cost 20-30% more for parts and servicing.

faq.q: Is the Yamaha Tracer 700 good for long-distance UK touring?
faq.a: The Tracer 700 is excellent for UK touring with engaging handling and a characterful engine. The seat can get firm after 4+ hours, so budget for an aftermarket option if planning regular 300+ mile days. Weather protection is good but benefits from a taller aftermarket screen.

faq.q: Should I buy a sports tourer or adventure bike for UK touring?
faq.a: Adventure bikes (V-Strom, Versys, Tiger) offer better weather protection, upright comfort, and easier luggage mounting. Sports tourers (VFR800, GTR1400) provide sportier handling and higher speeds but with more aggressive riding positions. For pure British touring with variable weather, adventure bikes edge it.

faq.q: What mileage is acceptable for a touring bike under £5000?
faq.a: 20,000-40,000 miles is the sweet spot for value versus condition. Japanese bikes regularly exceed 60,000+ miles with proper maintenance. Focus on complete service history rather than raw mileage - a well-maintained 35,000 mile bike is better than a neglected 15,000 mile example.

# Best Touring Motorcycle Under £5000 UK: My Top Picks for 2026

Right, let's talk about something close to my heart – finding a proper touring bike without having to sell a kidney. I've spent years riding across Britain on all sorts of machinery, and I can tell you straight: you don't need to drop ten grand to have brilliant touring adventures. The used market is absolutely packed with solid bikes that'll take you from Cornwall to the Highlands without drama, and £5000 is actually a sweet spot where you get proper quality without the new bike depreciation.

I'm writing this in 2026, and the market's shifted a bit since a few years back. Brexit affected import costs, but the flip side is there are loads of well-maintained bikes from riders who've upgraded or hung up their helmets. I've ridden most of these recommendations personally – some I've owned, others I've borrowed from mates or tested on everything from the A537 Cat and Fiddle to week-long trips up the NC500.

What Makes a Good Touring Bike Under £5K?

Before I get into specific models, let me share what I've learned matters most when you're spending full days in the saddle across British roads. Comfort's obviously top of the list – if your backside's numb by Scotch Corner, you're on the wrong bike. But there's more to it than just a plush seat.

You want something reliable. Properly reliable. Breaking down in the Highlands when it's chucking it down isn't romantic, it's miserable. I look for bikes with proven engines, good parts availability, and reasonable service intervals. The best touring bike is the one that actually gets you there.

Weather protection matters more than you'd think. Yeah, we've all got decent gear now, but a bike with good wind protection means you arrive less knackered. I've ridden naked bikes on tours and while it's doable, a proper screen makes motorway slogs infinitely more pleasant.

"In the UK touring market, the bikes that depreciated hardest often make the best value buys – they were brilliant when new, and they're still brilliant now, just cheaper."

Luggage capability is essential. Either the bike needs a good rack system, or pannier mounts that don't cost a fortune. I've bodged luggage onto sports bikes before, and trust me, it's not worth the aggravation when you can buy something designed for it.

My Top Picks for Touring Under £5000

Suzuki V-Strom 650 (2007-2016)

I'm putting this first because it's probably the most sensible choice, and I've covered serious miles on these. You'll find 2012-2015 models comfortably within budget, often with luggage already fitted. The V-twin engine is bulletproof – I've known V-Stroms with over 80,000 miles still running sweet.

The weather protection is brilliant, the seat's good for 300-mile days, and the upright position means you can actually see over hedgerows on B-roads. I've taken one through Welsh valleys in torrential rain and up to the Highlands in August (which also meant rain, let's be honest), and it just gets on with the job.

The adjustable screen works well, panniers are cheap and plentiful, and every small-town garage can work on it. It's not exciting, but excitement at 3pm on day four of a tour when you're tired and wet isn't what you want. You want to arrive. The V-Strom does that.

Watch for: tired suspension on higher-mileage examples, and check the chain and sprockets have been maintained properly. Budget around £3,000-£4,500 depending on mileage and condition.

Kawasaki Versys 650 (2010-2018)

The Versys is the V-Strom's slightly sportier cousin. Same parallel-twin philosophy, but it feels a bit more eager, a bit more involving. I've ridden one from Manchester to Edinburgh and back in a weekend, and while my mate on his V-Strom got there just as comfortably, I had a bit more fun on the twisty bits.

The engine's from the ER-6, which means it's been proven in everything from commuters to track day bikes. Parts are everywhere, and reliability is solid. The riding position's great for all-day comfort, though I'd say the seat's not quite as plush as the Suzuki's straight out of the box.

Wind protection's acceptable but not class-leading. On motorways above 80mph (not that we'd do that, officer), you feel the buffeting more than on some rivals. But on A-roads and through places like the Island to Highlands route, it's absolutely brilliant.

Watch for: The older models had some reports of electrical gremlins, though nothing serious. Check all the lights and switches work properly. Prices range from £3,200 to £4,800 for good examples.

Honda CB500X (2013-2018)

Honda reliability in a lightweight, easy-to-ride package. I rode a 2015 model for a whole summer, and while it's not the fastest thing on the road, it's one of the most pleasant. The parallel-twin is smooth, economical (I regularly saw 70+ mpg), and utterly dependable.

It's properly light compared to the bigger adventure bikes, which makes it brilliant for newer tourers or anyone who doesn't fancy wrestling a 250kg monster around petrol station forecourts. The low seat height means shorter riders can get both feet flat down, which makes a real difference when you're tired at the end of a long day.

The standard screen's a bit short for my liking – I'm 6'1" and got more wind blast than I'd prefer. But aftermarket screens are cheap and effective. Luggage mounts are solid, and you'll find loads of touring accessories available.

Watch for: Not much, honestly. These are Honda-reliable. Check service history is complete, as some were used by schools and rode hard by learners. Expect to pay £3,500-£4,800.

Yamaha Tracer 700 (2016-2019)

If you want something with a bit more character, the Tracer's where it's at. That CP2 engine (from the MT-07) has proper personality – it's a crossplane twin that feels engaging every time you crack the throttle. I've ridden these through the Yorkshire Dales and along the North Coast 500, and they never get boring.

The handling's brilliant for a touring bike. It's based on the MT-07, so it's got that lightweight, flickable chassis that makes B-road blasts an absolute joy. Weather protection is good, though like most in this class, an aftermarket screen helps on longer motorway stints.

Comfort's decent, though the seat can get a bit firm after four hours. I'd budget for an aftermarket option if you're planning regular long days. Panniers and luggage solutions are readily available – check out SportsBikeShop for good options on Yamaha luggage systems.

Watch for: Early models had some issues with the TFT display in very cold weather. Most were fixed under warranty, but worth checking. Budget £4,200-£5,000 for 2016-2017 models.

Triumph Tiger 800 (2011-2014)

Stretching the budget a bit here, but if you can find a well-maintained early 800, they're fantastic bikes. The triple engine is an absolute peach – smooth, powerful enough for two-up touring, and that Triumph sound is properly addictive.

I borrowed a mate's 2012 XC for a week in Scotland, and it was brilliant. Comfortable, planted on everything from motorways to muddy forest tracks, and the build quality felt genuinely premium. The shaft drive on some models is lovely for touring – no chain maintenance on multi-day trips.

Weather protection is excellent, the screen adjusts easily (even with gloves on), and the riding position is spot-on for long days. These were £10k+ bikes new, so getting one for half that feels like proper value.

Watch for: They're more complex than the Japanese alternatives, so service history is crucial. Check for any electrical issues, and budget for potentially pricier maintenance. Prices vary wildly based on condition – £4,000-£5,500 is the realistic range.

What About Sports Tourers?

I know some of you are thinking "what about a VFR800 or an older FJR1300?" and yeah, these are legitimate options. I've toured on both, and they're brilliant in their own way.

Honda VFR800 (2002-2013)

The VFR's a proper do-it-all bike. V4 engine that's smooth as silk, gear-driven cams that sound glorious, and build quality that justifies Honda's reputation. Older VTEC models (2002-2013) are well within budget, and they're still brilliant bikes.

The downside for pure touring is the riding position's more aggressive than adventure bikes. You're leaned further forward, which some people love and others find tiring on full days. I'm fine with it, but I've got mates who prefer the upright stance of ADV bikes.

Weather protection's good, and factory panniers are available secondhand fairly easily. These bikes look after you in British weather – heated grips were standard on many models, and the fairing keeps the worst off you.

Watch for: VTEC versions are brilliant but slightly more complex. The exhaust collector can corrode, and replacement isn't cheap. Service intervals are reasonable but valve clearances need checking. £3,000-£4,500 gets you a good one.

Kawasaki GTR1400/Concours 14 (2008-2015)

If you can find one under £5k (just about possible for older examples), these are phenomenal touring machines. Big, fast, comfortable, and built to eat motorway miles. I've ridden one from London to Inverness in a day, and arrived less tired than I've been after some 200-mile trips on less suitable bikes.

The shaft drive is maintenance-free, the luggage is massive, and the weather protection is class-leading. Two-up touring is effortless, and the power means overtaking on A-roads is easy and safe.

The downside is weight – they're proper heavy, which means tight manoeuvring takes effort and dropping one would be expensive. They're also big bikes for narrow British roads and village centres.

Watch for: Age-related issues on early models – suspension can need refreshing, and brake components need checking. £4,500-£5,500 for 2008-2010 models.

What I'd Actually Buy

If it were my £5000 and I was buying tomorrow? I'd get a 2013-2015 Suzuki V-Strom 650 with 20,000-30,000 miles and full service history. They're everywhere, they're reliable, parts are cheap, and they just work. Then I'd spend the remaining budget on good luggage, maybe some heated grips, and fuel for actually going places.

If I wanted something more exciting, I'd go for the Yamaha Tracer 700. That engine has character, and it makes you smile on every ride. It's nearly as practical as the V-Strom but way more engaging.

For someone shorter or newer to touring, the CB500X is brilliant. For someone who wants premium feels and doesn't mind potentially higher maintenance costs, the Tiger 800.

Essential Checks When Buying

Whatever you choose, these checks are non-negotiable. I've been stung before, and I don't want you making the same mistakes.

  • Full service history – not negotiable for bikes at this price point. Missing services mean potential problems.
  • Check the chain, sprockets, and brake components – these tell you how the bike's been maintained.
  • Tyres should be decent and evenly worn. Odd wear patterns suggest suspension issues.
  • Take it for a proper test ride – 15 minutes minimum, including motorway if possible.
  • Check all electrical components work, especially heated grips and ABS.
  • Look for crash damage – scratched bar ends and levers are normal, but check frame sliders and panels.
  • HPI check it – stolen bike recovery stories aren't as romantic as they sound.

Setting Up for British Touring

Once you've bought your bike, you'll want to set it up properly. I've got a detailed touring gear guide, but here are the immediate priorities.

First, sort the luggage. Hard panniers are brilliant for British weather – everything stays dry even when you forget to pack your waterproof covers (yes, I've done this). Soft luggage is cheaper and lighter, but you'll need to be more careful about waterproofing.

Second, get the suspension set up for your weight and typical load. Most bikes come with suspension set for an average 75kg rider, and very few of us match that when we're in full gear with luggage. Proper suspension setup transformed my last tour – the bike handled better and was way more comfortable.

Third, consider a tank bag. Having your phone, snacks, and camera easily accessible makes a huge difference on tour. I use mine constantly – maps, taking photos at viewpoints, grabbing a cereal bar without stopping.

Use our touring packing checklist to make sure you've got everything covered before your first big trip.

Running Costs Matter

Don't just think about the purchase price. I learned this the expensive way with an older BMW – cheap to buy, eye-watering to maintain.

The Japanese bikes I've recommended are all reasonable to run. Insurance should be £200-400 for most riders (check your own quotes, obviously). Services range from £150-300 depending on the bike and whether you DIY. Chain and sprockets are £150-250 when they need doing. Tyres are £200-300 for decent touring rubber fitted.

The Tigers and VFRs cost a bit more – parts are pricier, and specialists often charge higher labour rates. Not prohibitive, just worth factoring in.

Fuel economy varies – the CB500X will do 70mpg, the GTR1400 more like 45mpg. On a 3,000 mile tour, that's the difference between £250 and £400 in fuel at current prices.

Real-World British Touring Reality

Here's the thing nobody tells you: any bike on this list will tour Britain brilliantly. The differences matter less than you think once you're actually riding.

I've done the NC500 on a V-Strom. Brilliant. I've done Welsh loops on a VFR. Also brilliant. I've crossed to Scotland on a CB500X in February (less brilliant, but the bike was fine, the weather was horrific).

What matters more is sorting your gear properly, planning routes that match your riding style, and maintaining the bike well. A £3,000 V-Strom that's properly serviced and set up will give you better tours than a £5,000 bike you've neglected.

British weather means waterproofs that actually work, gear that layers properly, and accepting that some days will be wet. Scottish summer tours mean midges – seriously, pack repellent. English bank holiday tours mean traffic – plan routes that avoid motorways when possible.

Final Thoughts and Next Steps

Right, that's probably more than you wanted to know about touring bikes under £5k. The bottom line is this: the market's brilliant right now for riders on this budget. You can get a proper, sorted touring bike that'll serve you for years.

My advice? Decide what kind of riding appeals most. If it's adventure touring with some off-road capability, go V-Strom or Versys. If it's spirited road touring, look at the Tracer or VFR. If it's comfort-first mile munching, consider the bigger sports tourers.

Then get out there and actually use it. The best touring bike is the one you actually tour on. Start with weekend trips, build up to longer adventures, and use our route planning tools at Build a Route to discover brilliant roads across Britain.

See you out there. And if you spot me on my V-Strom somewhere in the Highlands, give us a nod. Read our Best Touring Motorcycle for Beginners (2026) | VisorUp guide for more.
